title: Bird Watching
strapline: Stand very still, keep your voice low — and let the robin come to the feeder you filled.
intent: Birds bring wild living things right up to the window, and provision built around them gives children daily, real encounters with the natural world.
Filling feeders and keeping the water topped up teaches that living things have needs, and that caring for them is a real and repeated responsibility.
Watching quietly and patiently grows stillness, focus and careful observation — the opposite skills to the ones most of the day asks for.
Counting the visitors, noticing who is biggest, who comes most often and who chases whom is natural mathematics and early data.
Children learn real knowledge of the world — which birds visit, what they eat, the sounds they make, how the visitors change with the seasons.
Watching, naming and describing pours in language — robin, blackbird, feather, beak, perch, flutter, peck.
implementation: Set up feeders and a shallow water dish where children can see them from a window, and make filling and topping-up a shared daily job.
Create a quiet watching spot — a bench, cushions, binoculars (real or made), a chart of the birds you might see.
Model the low, patient talk: 'Sshh — look, something's landed. Let's keep really still and see what it does.'
Weave in maths and record-keeping — a simple tally of who visits, count how many at the feeder, spot which bird is bigger than the robin.
Feed in real knowledge as you watch — this one's a blackbird, it likes the ground, listen to its song — and keep bird books nearby.
Follow the seasons: make fat-balls for cold mornings, watch for nest-building in spring, and notice how the visitors change through the year.
key_questions: Sshh — something's landed. What do you think it will do?
How many birds can you count at the feeder?
Which one is bigger than the robin?
What do you think the birds need us to give them?
Can you hear that song — which bird do you think it is?

impact.text: Children learn that living things have needs and take real responsibility for filling the feeders.
Children watch quietly and patiently, growing stillness, focus and careful observation.
Children count the visitors and keep a simple tally, comparing who comes most and who is biggest.
Children build real knowledge of the birds, their food and songs, and how visitors change with the seasons.
Children name and describe what they see, gaining words like robin, feather, beak, perch, flutter.

enhancements: A quiet watching bench with cushions, real or made binoculars and a chart of the birds to spot.
A daily tally of who visits, kept over the week and talked about together.
Fat-balls and seed cakes made for cold mornings and hung where children can watch.
Bird books and a nest-building watch through spring.
A window feeder so the closest visitors can be studied up close.

playing_exploring: Children watch real wild birds up close and follow their curiosity about who visits and what they do.
They use eyes and ears carefully, tuning in to small movements and quiet sounds.
active_learning: Children keep still and wait, holding their attention for a bird that may take its time to come — and keep the feeders filled day after day.
creating_thinking: Children notice patterns in who visits and when, and begin to explain what the birds are doing and why.
